summary: Discovery call to assess model selection needs for Novus AI. Key themes: context length requirements (multi-document conversations, 64k target), multilingual support (English/Spanish/Japanese), tool-calling / function-calling for retrieval and external APIs, and deployment mode options (hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC). Customer is leaning toward Dedicated for predictable throughput but needs answers on latency/cost tradeoffs and security compliance (SOC2, SAML, KMS). Next steps: pricing, benchmark template, tech deep-dive.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-26 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Sarah Kim (Redwood AE), Ethan Lopez (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (Novus CTO), Maya Chen (Novus Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Novus DevOps)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
- Novus evaluates models for a customer-facing assistant that must handle long multi-doc contexts (~60k tokens), support English/Spanish/Japanese, and call tools/APIs for booking/CRM lookups.
- Discussed Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private with tradeoffs: latency, cost, data residency.
- Action items and follow ups agreed.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sarah (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sarah, AE on the account, with Ethan our SE. How are you all doing?
[00:04] Raj (Novus): Good, thanks. Excited to talk through model choices. We've been evaluating a couple of open models and also looking at the hosted providers.
[00:10] Maya (Novus): Hi, yeah we've got a laundry list — context length, multilingual, and we really need tool-calling for CRM and calendar actions.
[00:16] Ethan (Redwood): Great. Can you walk us through the primary user flow and what you mean by multi-doc context?
[00:20] Raj: Sure. So imagine a customer support assistant that ingests several documents — purchase history, support thread, product manual — and then needs to synthesize answers. The ask is roughly a 50-64k token window to avoid losing earlier context.
[00:30] Maya: And we need Spanish and Japanese parity — not just translation but native performance for generation and classification.
[00:36] Liam (Novus): From infra side we care about latency SLOs — median response under 600ms for short prompts, and we can tolerate up to 2-3s for longer multi-doc answers. Cost is important too; if we go hosted at scale the per-token costs add up.
[00:48] Ethan: Understood. So two big dimensions: model architecture & context length, and deployment mode (hosted/dedicated/private). For context length we have options: some open models support long context natively or via chunking + retrieval. Others require longer context variants or special kernel optimizations.
[01:02] Raj: Can you give examples? Like Llama-type models vs Mistral vs other open weights?
[01:06] Ethan: Yeah, roughly: Llama-3 family and some LLama derivatives have long context variants up to 128k with the right runtime; Mistral has strong locality but historically shorter windows though there are long-context forks. There's also newer community models optimized for long-range attention. Redwood maintains a catalog of tested variants and will surface performance tradeoffs — latency, memory, and cost.
[01:24] Sarah: One quick question on tool-calling: are you planning developer-invoked API calls (server-side) or end user-facing function calls from the model? That impacts whether we use function-calling style or orchestrate tools outside the model.
[01:34] Maya: We want function-calling so the assistant can ask for a calendar slot and the system executes it, ideally with structured outputs.
[01:40] Ethan: Redwood supports function-calling / structured output patterns and you can host tool runtimes alongside the model or call them from your backend. We also have retriever integrations for RAG.
[01:49] Liam: On security — we need SOC2, SAML SSO, KMS for keys, audit logs. If we do Private deployment we may need VPC-only access.
[01:58] Sarah: All standard asks. For Dedicated we offer private capacity with network isolation and can integrate with customer KMS, and Private deployments can be fully VPC'd. Can you share the compliance checklist or any specific audit requirements?
[02:09] Raj: We'll share the vendor security questionnaire. Right now SOC2 and data residency in US/EU are the big ones, and we need encryption at rest with KMS keys we control.
[02:17] Ethan: Good. From the performance side, for 50-64k tokens the runtime needs to do KV cache management and efficient attention kernels. That often pushes you to larger GPUs or a sharding strategy. If latency is critical you might want a Dedicated pool sized for peak QPS.
[02:33] Raj: Is quantization compatible with long context? We want to reduce inference cost.
[02:37] Ethan: Yes — quantization like int8/int4 can reduce memory and cost, but for long context you need careful kernel support; some quantized kernels still keep efficient KV cache. We'll include recommended quant profiles per model.
[02:49] Maya: About multilingual — do open models vary a lot? We tested some models where Japanese quality dropped noticeably.
[02:55] Ethan: Right — not all models have balanced multilingual training. We recommend model benchmarks per language. Redwood can run per-language evals, and we can show tradeoffs: a multilingual model vs using translation + English-optimized model. That also affects latency and cost.
[03:10] Raj: Can you outline cost buckets for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private? Ballpark is fine.
[03:14] Sarah: Sure — hosted is easiest to start, pay-as-you-go per token — good for pilots. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools, so higher up-front commit but lower per-token cost and predictable latency. Private adds more ops/one-time setup cost for installation and ongoing license. We'll send detailed pricing but expect hosted to be higher per-token at scale.
[03:33] Liam: If we want predictable <600ms med latency for short prompts, which option should we lean to?
[03:38] Ethan: Dedicated — you can reserve capacity and tune batching policies to hit low tail latencies. Hosted can hit low med latencies but under noisy multi-tenant load you might see more variance unless you pay for premium tiers.
[03:50] Raj: For the model shortlist, could you recommend 2-3 variants we should test for our workload?
[03:55] Ethan: Absolutely. We'll propose: 1) Llama-3 long-context variant (64k / 128k where available) as a baseline; 2) A multilingual-capable open model (we'll pick one that tested well on JP/ES); 3) a smaller faster model for routing (e.g., a distilled variant) that we can use for initial classification and tool routing. We'll include quantization profiles for each.
[04:16] Maya: About tool-calling: need structured JSON outputs and a way to validate before executing. Is there a recommended pattern?
[04:21] Ethan: We recommend function-calling with a schema and a validation layer in your orchestration. Redwood's runtimes can return structured outputs and we integrate with your runtime to gate execution.
[04:31] Raj: Any limitations around PII redaction or data retention in hosted? We have strict retention rules for certain customers.
[04:36] Sarah: Hosted supports configurable retention windows; we also offer Dedicated with customer-controlled retention and Private with full data control. For high compliance requirements Private is typical.
[04:46] Liam: Network setup for Private — how invasive is it? We run on AWS; do you provide CloudFormation/Terraform?
[04:51] Ethan: We provide deployment automation and a customer install package — Terraform and helm charts for k8s where applicable. We'll share the ops runbook.
[04:58] Raj: For benchmarking, what do you need from us?
[05:01] Ethan: Sample prompts, language mix percentages, desired latencies (p50/p95), and a representative concurrency profile. We'll run end-to-end benchmarks on hosted and dedicated emulated setups.
[05:12] Sarah: Quick note — some transcription / doc: we'll send a benchmark template as a spreadsheet.
[05:16] Maya: Sounds good. A couple of concerns from product: hallucination risk on multi-doc summarization, and we need a plan for grounding via retrieval.
[05:23] Ethan: RAG with a dense or sparse retriever is recommended; we can also use chaining and answer verification patterns. We'll include recommended architectures in the follow-up doc.
[05:33] Raj: Competitors — we've tried Anthropic and OpenAI endpoints for a smaller pilot; cost and data residency were pain points. We're hoping an open-model + Redwood approach gives us control and cost benefits.
[05:43] Sarah: Understood. We'll make sure the follow-ups show apples-to-apples cost comparisons.
[05:47] Liam: One more on SSO — SAML and SCIM for provisioning?
[05:50] Ethan: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM are supported; RBAC and audit logs included on Dedicated/Private.
[05:57] Raj: What's the expected timeline if we wanted to start a pilot?
[06:00] Sarah: Pilot can start within 2-3 weeks for hosted. For Dedicated there's typically a 4-8 week provisioning depending on capacity and contractual lead time. Private installs depend on customer ops availability.
[06:10] Maya: Budget question — we'd prefer to start hosted for feature evaluation but move to Dedicated for scale. Is that a common path?
[06:15] Sarah: Very common. Start hosted to validate models and prompts, then move to Dedicated with a migration plan. We support model pinning so you can keep the same model configuration.
[06:24] Raj: Ok let's talk about evaluation criteria — accuracy on multi-doc QA, generation fluency in JP/ES, latency, cost per 1M tokens.
[06:30] Ethan: We'll configure the benchmark to capture all of that and include per-language BLEU/ROUGE-style metrics and human eval guidance.
[06:38] Sarah: Anything else from Novus team?
[06:41] Maya: Not right now. We'll collate prompts and a shortlist of sensitive customers to consider for retention rules.
[06:46] Raj: Cool. Thanks everyone.
[06:48] Sarah: Recap — Redwood to send pricing, security docs, benchmark template, and a shortlist of model variants + quantization recommendations. Novus to share prompt samples, language distribution, and vendor security questionnaire.
[06:58] Ethan: I'll also propose dates for a technical deep dive with your infra and ML teams.
[07:02] Liam: Thanks, looking forward.
[07:04] Sarah: Great — we'll follow up. Bye.

End of transcript.
